fixes.what: We the People layer item: credits and description cite the Census Bureau's 1791 return.

description:
House seats under the apportionment act of 14 April 1792 (105 seats, one for every 33,000 people counted under the three-fifths clause), with the seats each state would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full (SeatsIfAll) or not at all (SeatsIfNone).

The 1790 census figures are as tabulated in Wikipedia's article on the 1790 census, from the Census Bureau's Heads of Families volumes. Under the act's rule they reproduce every state's seats, which checks them.

Today's state outlines (Natural Earth, public domain), with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia.

Version 1.0 (14 October 2026).

The 1790 census figures are from the Census Bureau's Return of the Whole Number of Persons within the Several Districts of the United States (1791). Under the act's rule they reproduce every state's seats, which checks them.

Today's state outlines (Natural Earth, public domain), with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia.

Version 1.1 (23 October 2026).

fixes.what: Presidential (1800): pop-up title gives the year; pie numbers first; '1 vote'.

popupElements.text:
In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), {expression/adams}; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), {expression/jefferson}.

All electors' votes in 1800: {Votes1800}. Each elector cast two votes for president, so the votes add up to twice the number of electors.

Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 votes each, so the House of Representatives chose the president: Jefferson, on 17 February 1801. The 12th Amendment (1804) then gave electors separate votes for president and vice president.

{Note}

Source: National Archives
